Chapter Four: Worship as Formation—How Christian Practices Redirect Desire.
When you think about worship, maybe you picture a Sunday morning—singing familiar songs, bowing your head to pray, listening as someone reads from the Bible. It can feel like worship is just a way to show what’s already in your heart, right? But what if worship is a lot more than that?
Here’s something to pay attention to. Worship isn’t just an expression—it’s a practice that actually shapes what your heart longs for.
Imagine a small congregation, sitting together in an old, humble church. The pews have softened with years of use, the music might not be perfect, but there’s a comforting rhythm to the whole thing. People stand, sit, speak words that have echoed for centuries, and share bread and wine. Sure, these routines might seem a bit plain or even dull sometimes. But over time, they leave a deep impression. With each repetition, the heart learns something new—how to long for God, how to care for others, how to ground hope in something bigger than yourself.
Or picture a different scene: a family gathered around their table, lighting a single candle before dinner, pausing for a simple prayer, and sharing a quiet moment together. It’s a small ritual, but it can shape the entire evening. It reminds everyone that life is a gift, that gratitude is important, and that love lives in the smallest moments. Over the years, these habits form the heart, teaching it to love what’s good and true.
Worship isn’t just about saying what you already believe. It’s about forming new loves—redirecting your desires toward what truly brings life. Think of the practices of worship—singing, praying, confessing, sharing a meal—as exercises for your heart. They train you to love God and your neighbor, to find joy in serving others, and to keep hoping even when things are tough.
This kind of heart-shaping doesn’t happen all at once. It’s the result of small, faithful actions, repeated every week, year after year. These habits sink in deep, working in ways that words alone just can’t reach.
And worship isn’t limited to Sundays. You can weave these heart-shaping practices into everyday life—at the dinner table, in quiet moments, or through simple acts of kindness. They become anchors, quietly reminding you what matters most.
It’s easy to overlook the power of these everyday rituals. They might seem ordinary, maybe even forgettable. But over time, they form your heart, teaching you to love what’s truly worth loving. They offer a counter-story to what the world tells you—a new vision of what the good life can be.
So if you’re thinking about spiritual formation, remember: it’s about more than just ideas. It’s about habits—practices that guide your heart toward what’s truly good. Worship is the training ground for this kind of transformation—a space where your desires are shaped, redirected, and renewed.
